summary:
Krasnoyarsk Krai stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation in full. The sources identify no deviation from that framework at the level of Krasnoyarsk Krai material sufficient to score separately, and the division is therefore assessed at the national score.

Under that framework, same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned outright. Gender-marker changes on official documents are refused, legal gender recognition was banned in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute punishes public expression with administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence, and the expanded law reaches material that "justifies" gender transition. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation in it carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings expressly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. It assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, that the state is able but unwilling to protect them, and it affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war, and arbitrary law enforcement; the advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its symbols, of which about 98 were administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented well outside the major cities. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement wave is national in scope, so the operative risk for a visitor to Krasnoyarsk Krai is the country-wide pattern rather than any local initiative. Volume figures such as the eighteenfold growth in propaganda-law cases and the 60 million rubles collected in fines over two years indicate that charges are being brought routinely, not selectively.

Raids on venues associated with LGBTQ+ patrons occurred in Moscow within 48 hours of the Supreme Court designation, and the pattern of arrests, club raids and extremism charges continued through 2025, meaning the practical risk of being present in a social setting is not confined to a single date or city.

Coercive treatment of transgender people has been documented in Siberia, in a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk where a transgender woman was held for nine months. This places the documented coercion geographically near Krasnoyarsk Krai rather than only in European Russia.

Deaths in pretrial detention of people held on extremism-related charges, together with a Level 4 travel advisory citing wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, indicate that the risk does not end at arrest.
localsOnly:
Russian residents face the same prohibitions as visitors, with additional exposure through employment, housing and family settings in which discrimination has been assessed by the UK Home Office as capable of amounting to persecution, and in which the state is assessed as able but unwilling to protect.

At least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and residents carry a criminal record or administrative conviction risk for displaying banned symbols under article 20.3 and for alleged participation in the designated movement under article 282.2, with the latter carrying up to 12 years for the publishing-house staff charged.

Legal gender recognition and gender-marker changes on documents are unavailable to residents, so a resident's documents will continue to present a gender marker inconsistent with presentation at any checkpoint or identity check.

Residents who leave the country may qualify for protection abroad: the UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement, raids, prosecutions or facility conditions specific to Krasnoyarsk Krai; the regional layer rests entirely on national material and should be verified against Krasnoyarsk-specific reporting before being treated as a local finding.

The Human Rights Watch count of 101 extremism-related convictions is stated as of 30 June 2025 and the breakdown is given as approximate (about 98 administrative, three criminal); later totals are not sourced here.

The UK Home Office figures and assessments derive from a June 2025 note whose page was updated in August 2026, so the 139-people impact count covers 2022 to 2024 only and the current tally is unresolved.

Whether article 282.2 or article 20.3 has been applied to any person within Krasnoyarsk Krai is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The Meduza fine total is reported in rubles without a conversion at the date of reporting; the dollar figure carried elsewhere in the parent framework is not re-sourced in this inventory.
